title: vector — internals, push_back amortization

hook.scenario: You store a pointer to the first element of your `std::vector`. You then call `push_back()` a few times. When you try to read your pointer, the program crashes with a segmentation fault.
hook.question: If you never deleted the vector, why did the pointer to its data become invalid?

mental_model.intuition: `std::vector` is a dynamic array. When it runs out of space, it doesn't just expand—it buys a bigger house, copies all the furniture over, and burns down the old house.
mental_model.description: `std::vector` is the default sequence container in C++. It manages a contiguous block of memory on the heap. When that memory fills up, the vector must reallocate a larger block (usually double the size) and move all existing elements. This reallocation makes `push_back` an 'amortized O(1)' operation.

explanation:
Under the hood, a `std::vector` maintains three pointers: `begin` (start of data), `end` (end of active data), and `capacity` (end of allocated memory). The **size** is the number of active elements, while the **capacity** is the total number of elements it can hold before it must allocate more memory.

**Amortized O(1) Growth:**
When you call `push_back()` and `size == capacity`, the vector is full. It cannot just grow in place, because the adjacent memory might be owned by something else. Instead, it:
1. Allocates a completely new, larger array (usually 2x the current capacity).
2. Moves/copies all elements to the new array.
3. Deletes the old array.

While this reallocation is O(N), it happens so rarely that the *average* time per `push_back` remains O(1). This is called 'amortized' O(1).

**The Reallocation Trap:**
Because reallocation deletes the old array, **any pointers or references** pointing to elements inside the vector immediately become invalid (dangling). To prevent unnecessary reallocations and invalidation, always use `vec.reserve(N)` if you know roughly how many elements you will insert.

**Real-world Engineering:** If you must store references to elements but expect the vector to grow, **store integer indices** instead of pointers. Indices remain valid regardless of reallocation. A classic bug in game development is storing pointers to game entities inside a vector; when a new entity spawns and triggers a reallocation, all existing pointers danglingly crash the game. Use indices, or `reserve()` the max capacity upfront.

code_snippets.title: Reallocation and Invalidation
code_snippets.explanation: The moment `push_back` triggers a capacity increase, the vector moves all its data to a new heap location. The reference `firstElement` is left pointing to freed memory.

code_snippets.title: Using reserve() for performance
code_snippets.explanation: `reserve(N)` allocates memory ahead of time without changing the logical size of the vector. This prevents both performance hiccups and iterator/reference invalidation.

common_mistakes.title: Confusing reserve() with resize()
common_mistakes.explanation: `reserve(N)` only changes capacity (allocates memory). `resize(N)` changes both capacity AND size, actually instantiating `N` default objects (e.g., zeros). If you `resize(10)` and then `push_back(5)`, the `5` will be inserted at index 10, not index 0.

recall_questions.q: What is the difference between a vector's `size` and its `capacity`?
recall_questions.answer: `size` is the number of valid elements currently in the vector. `capacity` is the total number of elements the vector's current memory block can hold before needing to reallocate.

recall_questions.q: Why is `push_back` considered amortized O(1) rather than strict O(1)?
recall_questions.answer: Most of the time, `push_back` simply writes to the next available slot (strict O(1)). However, when capacity is reached, it must allocate a new array and copy all elements over (O(N)). Because it typically doubles the capacity, this O(N) cost is spread out over many O(1) operations, averaging to O(1).

It allocates enough contiguous memory to hold at least `N` elements, increasing the capacity without changing the logical size of the vector. This prevents reallocations while adding up to `N` elements.

oa_questions.question: A candidate reads 1 million integers from a file into a `std::vector` using a `while` loop and `push_back()`. The profiler shows the code spends 30% of its time allocating memory. How do you optimize this?
oa_questions.answer: If the file size or the number of elements is known beforehand, call `vec.reserve(1000000)` before the loop. This ensures exactly one memory allocation occurs, completely eliminating the reallocation overhead.
oa_questions.approach: Recognize the performance impact of repeated vector reallocations.

oa_questions.question: Is it safe to store pointers to elements of a `std::vector` inside another data structure?
oa_questions.answer: Generally, no. If the vector ever grows beyond its capacity, it will reallocate, invalidating every single stored pointer. If you must do this, either `reserve()` enough space so it never grows, or store indices (which remain valid) instead of pointers.
oa_questions.approach: Identify reference invalidation risks with dynamic arrays.

key_points.title: Contiguous memory is king
key_points.detail: `std::vector` is the fastest container because it is cache-friendly. It should be your default choice.

key_points.title: Beware reallocation
key_points.detail: Growth means moving data. Reallocation invalidates all pointers, references, and iterators to the vector's elements.
